utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber, more specifically I, apologise for the late start. Partly due to the consequences of frost. Before an opportunity will be given to the Prosecution to call its next witness, we'd like first to give an opportunity, 11 minutes for the Defence, to further -- make further oral submissions on scheduling issues. Who's first? Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. May it please the Court. Thank you. Your Honour I will have to some submissions to make, and I think the colleagues, the other two teams, will also have some very brief submissions to make. The submissions obviously concern the period of time that the Defence would like between the end of the Prosecution case and the commencement of the oral submissions under Rule 98 bis. And secondly the period of time between the end of the oral submissions under Rule 98 bis and the commencement of the first Defence case. In respect of the first matter, that is the time between end of Prosecution case and the beginning of the Rule 98 bis submissions, we would request a period of 15 working days. For the second period, the period between the end of the Rule 98 bis submissions and the commencement of the first Defence case, we would request 30 working days. Your Honours, I would like to bring to your attention six separate matters very briefly in respect of this application for time. The first matter is unique to the case of Ivan Cermak. You will recall that Mr. Kay was not appointed on this case until September of 2007. I was appointed in November of 2007 and Ms. Higgins in March of 2008. That is not Mr. Cermak's fault. You will recall that his old Defence team was removed by the Appeals Chamber in the summer of 2007. They had worked on the case for many years. Mr. Kay did ask for more time before the commencement of this trial. You will remember that he asked until October of 2008 before the case commenced. That time was not granted; we don't complain about that, but I think Your Honours will agree that we have kept pace with this case and now we need some time to prepare both for the Rule 98 bis and for the Defence case. The second matter, Your Honours, that I would like to bring to your attention is to remind you respectfully that this is a case of significant proportions. At the last count, I think before the witness that we just heard, there were 3475 exhibits, both Prosecution and Defence, and 88 Prosecution witnesses had been heard. This is a case of significant proportions, and I think it's fair to say that it falls into those categories of cases which are the larger and more complex cases. And if you look at the analysis that I sent to the Chamber and the Prosecution last Friday, I think you will find that what I've said is confirmed. Thirdly, the case has expanded throughout the Prosecution case. By that specifically I mean that there has been an increase in the number of exhibits, an increase in the number of documents and items on the Rule 65 ter list. The Defence teams have got to consider all of these matters, specifically within the Rule 98 bis submissions, and furthermore, in preparation for their Defence. The fourth matter that I would like to remind you of, Your Honours, and we don't take credit for this, but time has been used very efficiently in this case. If you look at the statistics that I have put together, you will find that in this case, we have sat five days a week for 57 percent of the time. Can you see in other cases, in other Chambers cases have not sat on that basis. Again, the Defence don't take credit for that. Perhaps the Judges and the Prosecution and the Defence together can take credit for that. But this is it true. We have used time very efficiently. And we would like to be given credit for that in terms of the time that we are granted for the Rule 98 bis submissions and our Defence case. The sixth matter that I'd like to raise is in respect of the Rule 98 bis application itself. And these -- these are words -- that's actually the fifth matter, not the sixth matter. But these were Mr. Kay's parting words to me as he left for the airport last night. He believes that we have a meritorious 98 bis application on behalf of our client Ivan Cermak, and we would respectively like to ask you for adequate time to prepare and -- those submissions to do our client justice and to do the best job that we can for him. The last matter, Your Honour, and I won't go through it, because I think it's fairly clear, the documents that I filed last Friday, we would like to draw your attention to the analysis that is being done and to the number of days granted in other cases in support of our application. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I don't have any further comments, and I think Mr. Misetic has comments to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, thank you very much for being succinct and very clear. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We joint with the Cermak Defence in terms of the amount of time requested. I would only add two points. One is we ask that the Chamber keep in mind the rule change that was enacted in February of 2008 pursuant to Rule 67(a) which now requires that the Defence make available to the Prosecutor the documents -- essentially the documents that the Defence will be introducing at trial. This is going to place a burden on us, whereas prior to that rule, we could have put documents together as the witnesses were coming up and disclosing them to the Prosecution. We are now required to essentially put our Defence case, in terms of documents, together before the commencement of the Defence case in chief. We obviously are going to endeavour to that so that our colleagues across the isle can have that material before the Defence case starts. However, that may impact in terms of comparing this case to other cases and when they start, the fact that we now have an additional burden that we will have to put all those documents together. The second practical issue for us is in terms of instructing experts and getting expert reports together. As the Chamber is aware, and there has been much litigation on this point, we have received addenda from the Prosecution well after the commencement of the trial, as recently as, I believe, November of 2008, which have, of course, prevented us from being able to instruct an expert to prepare a report given that theoretically speaking there may be even more witnesses coming up this month on the issue of shelling, for example. It hinders our ability to get experts to prepare their reports in time or to have complete reports, I should say. Given that additional factor of addenda to expert reports, we would ask that the Chamber also keep in mind that it is going to take us a little bit of extra time to get our expert reports together. Mr. Kehoe also would like to address one issue concerning the murder counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. We have addressed this to some degree before, but as a result of the appellate decision, we are back before the Chamber on the 189 deaths that the Prosecution has included as a schedule -- a clarification schedule in November of 2008. There are two issues. Number one, the Prosecution has to show that -- that obviously when they got this information and the prejudice that is involved, then the Chamber has to make a decision whether or not those items are in and out. That particular issue comes into play with the next witness. But based on Your Honours' decisions back in November, if Your Honours conclude that those killings are in, then we are going to need additional time to actually investigate those matters and go into them. I can tell Your Honour just from a brief bit of investigation on the matters that -- of those 189 killings while preparing for some of these forensic pathologists, there is any number of issues - I don't hasten to say problems - but issues with the Prosecution's submission to the Chamber and that clarification schedule. So it's going to take a significant amount of time to investigate those matters as well, if the Chamber maintains that -- or concludes that the Prosecution has gotten over the prejudice issue and those items should be included. That's -- I understand my colleagues have talked a bit about time-frames, but that particular time-frame makes the end of the Prosecution case quite difficult to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to add we fully agree with the presentation of both counsel, or all three counsel on the issue of timing, and the only other thing I would like to add is that the Chamber keep in mind the Easter holiday which for many of us is a traditional time for spending an at least a little bit of time with our family during the course of the break, so that's the only, sort of, personal thing that I have. But other than that, I agree completely with my counsel on their presentation. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't consider it perfectly personal, Mr. Kuzmanovic. I think we have all have the same experience, and we are also looking back at when this family time was not always available. Then, thank you for strictly keeping the time-limits. Any need to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next item. A motion is pending for a videolink. I think we have not heard from all Defence yet what their response is. Could I just make a short round. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We completely oppose the motion. I don't know if we should do there in private session but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we go into details, we certainly would have to do that. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. In view of the next witness, we have objections against the use of exhibits in more general terms, and also very specific ones filed, I think, yesterday; a list of some 30 approximately. I have some questions in that respect, first to the Prosecution. Part of the submission says that the victim does not appear in the indictment; does not appear in the clarification schedule, whatever the fate of that schedule may be; and the cause of death is unknown. Now, Mr. Margetts, what is the probative value of a person of who we do not know why he died and who does not appear in the indictment nor in the clarification schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first thing I understood that the objection of the Defence was that the victims didn't appear in the schedule to the indictment or the first clarification that was filed in March of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. The victims do appear in the further clarification schedule which is now, once again, before the Trial Chamber for consideration. So that's the relevance that they have in terms of the schedule of killings. They're in that further clarification schedule that was filed by Prosecution on the 16th July 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have this list of A to DD. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to say the victims do appear in the -- often it is claimed that they do not appear. That's one. And I was -- I think referring to one specific example, but I read it from my computer yesterday evening, so I'm trying to -- I thought there was one among them not appearing in the indictment, not appearing in the clarification schedule, and the cause of death unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think so, Judge. I think that Mr. Margetts is correct. Our objection is that these aren't in the indictment nor the first clarification schedule. But these are objections that are in the amended clarification schedule, the second clarification schedule that the Prosecution filed in July that was the subject of the November 2008 decision of the Chamber. And our objection, of course, was preceding on items which, at this juncture, are not before the Chamber. There is, of course, another larger objection with many, many of these that we have put in there that, geographically speaking, they simply were not in the Split Military District which -- and many of them were in the Gospic Military District. So if you look where the body was actually found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we find a variety of reasons. Sometimes being it was not where the Split Military District was, sometimes there were no Croatian soldiers, sometimes it is -- was where the special police was and not where the Split Military District was. So we find a variety. Sometimes it said who was in the area; sometimes it just says it's not the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. So to deal that with in one sentence, I find it a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree, Judge, that's why I tried to delineate all of the issues with each of these exhibits. I -- just with regard to in a particular area. The Prosecution in their amended schedule says that in P 1685 that an individual was killed in Donji Lapac on 8/5/1995. Excuse me, on the 5th of August, 1995. Now, the evidence before this Chamber, and I'm sure the Prosecution will agree, is there was simply no HV forces in Donji Lapac on the 5th of August of 1995. But nevertheless, that's what they have put forth in their clarification schedule. Have I any number of those. I just point that one out. We have other ones where, as I pointed out in there, there -- where the cause of death is natural causes. Yet, is in this schedule. There are several of those. I believe, I think, I have ten of unknown causes of death, where clearly some of them are natural causes. So we have a multitude of issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide me to natural causes, instead of no cause of death, in your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I actually -- frankly, I just put no cause of death, but can I tell you it is -- specifically it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the following reason, Mr. Kehoe. If you say no cause of death has been established, that means that through this report we may find some information about the body, although not a final answer to the question, why this person died. That can come from other evidence. We do not know yet. That would not automatically make it irrelevant. If there is an clear establishment that there was a natural cause of death then, of course, the body disqualifies for purposes of killing. So, therefore, it makes a difference if you put in your submissions it has no relevance because no cause of death has been established, that's different than cause of death was natural cause of death. That's makes a difference for looking at your submission and looking at the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, if we can harken back to my cross-examination of Dr. Clark where Your Honour cautioned me with regard to unknown causes and when we get into the unknown causes, and I asked the question does that -- it's equally plausible with the unknown cause that this person could have died from natural causes. Your Honour interjected and said, Well, of course, the Chamber knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perfectly. Could, could [Overlapping speakers] ... that's exactly -- you apparently have not understood my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm not saying that if there is an unknown cause of death that it means that the expert could not establish what the cause of death was. That, of course, leaves open at that moment in time not looking at any other evidence, that it could have been a natural cause as well. We'll have to see whether any other evidence comes up. Now, if, however an expert says this person died of a natural cause of death then, unless there is clearly contradicting evidence saying, no, he is wrong because I find five bullets in that body, then I would say that evidence is not probative in any way for killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my response to that, Judge, is based on -- Mr. President, your comments is one of relevance. And there is no question that because this is skeletonized remains and has very little flesh, some saponified flesh, but virtually no flesh, it's very difficult to tell organ damage, et cetera, as Dr. Clark said and I'm Dr. Baccard will as well. So they're not going to be able to say, Look at skeletonized remains what this person died from. However, they're not going to say, Looking at the skeletal remains, we don't have any idea how this person died. So we are in a position where the Prosecution has listed every body they have found, thrown them on a list, and then we're in the position of saying -- or they are saying, Oh, these are killings, and we're in a position to try to meet those. Now, this, of course, dove-tails with a larger problem in the investigation. But I have attempted to investigate many, many of the items that are set forth in this exhibit list from this witness we are to see. And there is into evidence in the record, nor in the 65 ter documents that the Prosecution has uploaded, on virtually none of them. Several of them there has been, and I can tell you exactly which ones there. Virtually the rest of them, there is none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can add another element to that. In addition to considering the forensic pathologist's evidence in context with the other evidence that has been brought before the Trial Chamber in relation to these deaths, the other factor that's -- that is indicative of the relevance of these autopsy reports is that the remains of the victims that have been the subject of these forensic examinations, and these persons are referred to in large part in Croatian official documents, and so another factor comes to bear; and that is the extent to which the deaths of these persons, be they unascertained, be they deaths by gun-shot injury, were within the notice of the accused. The accused knew of these deaths at the time, or alternatively, other members of the JCE or the subordinates knew of the deaths at the time. So it brings to bear another element of the case, that element being the notice case and the failure to investigate, the failure to ensure that the climate of fear generated by this large number of killings continued. So they failed to ensure that the Serbs felt safe on the territory. So in our submission there is another element here that's important in terms of addressing the evidence we have, in relation to these victims. The Prosecution has not at all listed all of the killings that they are aware of. They have listed the killings that are relevant to elements that are in the indictment, and one of those elements is knowledge and the failure to respond and protect the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am needless to say, shocked by that submission. I mean, the Prosecution knows full well that deaths in a cemetery or in an area mean nothing. They have not presented one iota of evidence that General Gotovina had any knowledge of any murder or criminal activity, zero. None. They have nothing before the Chamber. What this is, what this is, is an attempt to put fort a litany of bodies to essentially shock the Chamber, so the Chamber concludes that something untoward happened, i.e., murder, that the accused must have had knowledge of, and there is no evidence to support that. And I offer to -- to Mr. Margetts to present some evidence that the accused knew of these particular items, that they knew that people were murdered. The Prosecution can't even say when these people were buried. It is it -- they have yet addressed one of the larger issues here, Mr. President, is that the - I don't want say the vast majority - that almost 50 percent of these bodies were found in a different Military District. They were not in the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add something to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What is happening here is essentially the burden of proof is being reversed. These people were killed, and you have to proof that you had nothing do with it. That's not the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not aware that the Prosecution is in a position to reverse the burden of proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's factually what they're trying to attempt to do here, Your Honour. By putting these people on this list and giving us either -- you know, you can see on the annex, for example. It filed in July, and I can just give you an example. Number 53 on the annex which is P1553 says that this particular person was killed on 5th August, and then P1553, it says it was the 10th of August. How am I suppose to cross-examine a pathologist who knows nothing about that on that particular issue? Whose burden is that? Is that my burden? Or is that the Prosecution's burden? What's happening here essentially, and one of the reasons I sent an e-mail to Mr. Margetts last night with respect to the Appeals Chamber's decision remanding the further clarification to the Trial Chamber was, how can you present evidence that the Appeals Chamber said isn't necessarily in play because the Trial Chamber hasn't decided the issue of the remand yet on the two issues that the Appeals Chamber said the Trial Chamber must decide. Now obviously, it was a week and two days ago that the Trial Chamber got this, and no one expects the Trial Chamber to make a decision so quickly given all things that have been going on. But how can evidence be presented and exhibits be presented on issues that still are still not decided with this particular witness. And then how are we to cross-examine on that? For this particular witness to testify on issues related -- on issued related to the clarification that was filed in July, given the fact that there has been no decision from the Trial Chamber on this, I think it is premature for this particular witness to testify now on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it is not a debating club here, but it is a court of law. Mr. Margetts, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Briefly please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I 'all deal with is that Mr. Kehoe referred to the fact that he asserts that these killings took place outside the Split Military District. We would say the relevant area that he should be referring to is the area described in the indictment, which is not defined by the Military District but is defined by the municipality. The second issue is that Mr. Kehoe claims there has been no evidence in relation to the knowledge of the accused of these killings. We differ on that. We say that contemporaneous documents demonstrate abundantly that the accused and other members of JCE were informed in writing about the killings of these civilians, and they were informed also you've heard witness testimony to the fact that these matters were discussed in meetings with the accused. The third issue I'd deal with is the issue of this matter being referred back, an issue raised by Mr. Kuzmanovic. The clarification, the further clarification of July 2008 that sets out -- lists all of these victims, it was challenged on the 24th of July, by the Gotovina Defence. The Trial Chamber made a decision. The Appeals Chamber has now requested that that decision count -- well, has ordered that that decision come back to the Trial Chamber. We're in no different position today than we were on the 24th of July. And we have carried on this trial since the 24th of July, when the Defence objections to the further clarification were on the record within. And it was within the hands of the Trial Chamber as to whether the further clarification of the Prosecution would be allowed. Again, this is an interlocutory matter before the Trial Chamber, and there's no merit we say whatsoever, in the current application that the Defence have belatedly put before you, and the reasons being that, effectively, it is just an interlocutory application for the Trial Chamber to consider. It's not a ground for adjournment of the proceeding which is effectively what they seek. Because following witnesses will be talking about killings that fall within the further clarification. So we say this is a wholly meritorious application and should be dismissed. And I go back to the other issue, and it's not just the further clarification that the evidence of Dr. Baccard is relevant to. It's relevant to the general elements of widespread and systematic, the proof of how many people, how many civilians were killed. It's also relevant to the issue that I raised before, for instance, I can quote the paragraphs of the indictment, paragraph 17(D) to (E) that deal with the failure of the accused to act, the failure of the accused having notice that all of these people were being killed, the failure of the accused to stop those killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you to be brief, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One brief comment, just very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I would also like you to respond specifically on the issue raised by Mr. Margetts as to the geographical scope of the indictment as the determining factor, rather than the area of responsibility of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would include that in your answer within the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My response to that is twofold. They have put a broad reach in the indictment and covered areas that were in the Gospic Military District that have no application to our client with no responsibility whatsoever. Those -- to the extent that the Prosecution is arguing that HV troops committed crimes in a different sector, that cannot be lead at the feet of General Gotovina. The more serious problem with the argument of Mr. Margetts is not one of deaths. It's not one of people dying because people die in a war. The question here is murder, and knowledge of murder. They are put forth no evidence whatsoever, zero, that General Gotovina had knowledge of murders. And that is the issue here. They have nothing in that regard. Now to compound the problem, they are saying, We're going to put before this Chamber issues of killings where there has been no evidence of -- that it is in fact a murder and -- it takes place in an entirely Military District. Killing itself, people dying, is not a crime. What is a crime is murder. And the Prosecution has put forth no evidence with regard to General Gotovina of knowledge of any of these murders. None. And they have simply tried to compound this problem by adding to people's deaths in areas that are not even under his command and control. It is extremely prejudicial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add to that the specific issue regarding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, May I -- before I give you an opportunity to do so, Mr. Kehoe, you said well, not even in the Split Military District, Gospic, but often I do not find a positive determination of in whose area of responsibility the incident may have happened. Sometimes it is specifically said it was in the area of responsibility of the special police and not of the Split Military District which is not the same as Gospic. And I can imagine that Mr. Kuzmanovic would like to perhaps also comment on that part of the submissions made by the Gotovina Defence. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there was a corrigendum filed by Gotovina Defence on the issue of area of responsibility specifically related to the special police so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just have a look. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the corrigendum was filed last night, Your Honour. Our courtesy copy was sent last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check then whether it reached [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I can address that issue anyway, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Two things. First, I want to relate back to the issue of area of responsibility. We can all agree that Korenica is not in any area of responsibility relating to this indictment, yet one of the exhumations that takes place is from the cemetery in Korenica. And we have to deal with that in our list of additional scheduled killings, among other things, and in Dr. Baccard's report. My question would be, How is that applicable to us in this case? An exhumation in a cemetery that is nowhere near where our clients were operating. That's number one. Number two, as another example, one of the exhibits, P1554 discusses the death of someone who was in uniform which is a soldier, and the cause of death is it most likely an explosive injury to the head, trunk, and limbs. How is that a murder? How is that a murder? That's out of the additional list of scheduled of killings. There are 189 additional scheduled killings. And for us to have to deal with this particular witness on 189 additional scheduled killings going through these one by one under the circumstances in which that further clarification still hasn't been effectively decided is a very difficult thing to do in cross-examination. Now, the issue of area of responsibility. The Chamber will recall that in this particular area, for example, in Gracac, the special police did not have effective control of territory. They had an axis of attack. And they were under the command of the Main Staff of the Croatian military. Now if you look, for example, at the date of the finding of the body of this particular person in P1554, on the road between Gracac and Otric, the date of the finding of the body was August 10th. The special police was not there on August 10th. The war diary of the special police, which has been submitted as an exhibit, and our response, specifically says when and where special police were operating. They were not in this area on August 10th of 1995. Those are the kinds of things that, unfortunately, we're going to have to go through in cross-examination of this particular witness to show that we, either, for example, the special police was not present with respect to this particular exhibit P1554, or there are some other circumstance. That's what we're going to have to do, given the description in every single autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless the witness would state in a more general way that he has not any knowledge, Mr. Kehoe would say, none, zero, about - I usually leave it to not any knowledge - to the whereabouts of whatever units or whatever troops, and that the only thing he did, is that this is information he can't confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I definitely understand that, but the whole proposition of use of this witness and these exhibits is an attempt to establish responsibility on our three individual clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or to establish some factual -- some facts that were observed by -- by the expert. Now, that might keep you even more divided. Mr. Kehoe said that he was shocked, and he, a few lines later, said that the Prosecution was aiming at shocking the Chamber. I don't know whether there's any relationship between perhaps easily being shocked and expectations that others will be shocked. I'm not saying that Mr. Kehoe was easily shocked, but at least he was shocked. We have to look at the -- what has been submitted to the Chamber. Where is the line between being convinced, being surprised, being shocked, there is a wide variety of effects. And I do understand that where Mr. Margetts claims that he has honest intentions to assist the Chamber rather than to mislead the Chamber, that that is not a shared view -- that that view is not shared by the Defence. That is perfectly clear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning anybody's honesty, Your Honour. My position is that when the Appeals Chamber makes a decision remanding whether or not 189 additional killings can be the subject of the amended schedule, and the Trial Chamber has not yet decided that issue, and the Prosecution wants to go ahead and put evidence in there through this witness anyway, I think there is some issue there that I have with that, from an officer of the court standpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you may be very brief. You would like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to respond to a number of those matters. The first thing is that what we have done, is we have redacted from Dr. Baccard's report all references to the Korenica victims, the reason being that none of them appear in any of the clarifications or schedules we have filed. The second thing is, I think, Mr. President, you have dealt with it entirely. It seems to me that Mr. Kuzmanovic is arguing about merits of the case and ultimate submissions as to the linkage to his accused, rather than the relevance of this specific evidence relating to the limits of what this specific witness can testify about. He was in a mortuary in 2002; he made observations about the remains. That is what his evidence is about, and it doesn't extend further. In terms of this being new to the Defence, that there are 189 killings, the Prosecution never, never limited the number of killings. There was a schedule to the indictment; there was a clarification in March 2007; there was a further clarification in March of 2008. These killings were always the subject of this proceeding, and they were expressly identified by the Prosecution to aid the parties, and the parties should have been addressing these killings well before July 2008. In July 2008 assistance was given to the parties and the Trial Chamber with this further identification. The proceeding continued from July 2008, while the Trial Chamber's decision -- were awaiting the decision. There is no reason today for this proceeding to be effectively adjourned and the evidence of this witness on these matters not to be heard. There is no prejudice whatsoever to the Defence, should this witness, in addition to the 11 killings that he will refer to in the schedule and the clarification, if he also refers to killings that are in the further clarification. There is no prejudice. We're in no different position to the position we were in, in July 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It took me a while to find the example I referred to earlier. That is, not in the indictment, not in the clarification schedule, and the cause of death unknown. Because that is one of the examples I said I thought I would have found one. Mr. Margetts, under M we find 65 ter 6050, cause of death unknown. Not in the indictment, not in the clarification schedule, and it was added not occurring in the area of the Split Military District. So apart from to what extent that is the determining geographical factor, but what is the probative value of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We emphasise the -- the extent to which this witness can testify about circumstances of death. This witness can testify about cause of death, well, insofar as he can ascertain it and be certain of it from the remains. Where the cause of death is unknown, it doesn't mean that there aren't features that are observed by this witness about the body that would alert those that disposed of the body, and we have heard a lot of the evidence about the systematic disposal of the bodies, that there should have been an inquiry into it. Now if that inquiry eventually came up with the same conclusion that Dr. Baccard came -- or that Strinovic or the Croatian examiners arrived at after a proper examination, taking into the account circumstances, the criminal investigation, and all those things, that is one issue. What we have here is a forensic pathologist who can say that, In 2002, I couldn't ascertain the cause of death. Now if in 1995 proper steps had been taken, that is it not dispositive of whether or not the accused and those subordinate to them, if they had done what they're obliged to do, would have been able to determine that cause of death. So the findings of this witness are variously strong as to cause of death. Finding that there's none ascertained cause of death, does not exclude his evidence as being evidence of value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The procedural order would that we have heard the objections; we have heard the response; we have heard this in two or three rounds. The Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer to consider the matter during the break. We would then have a rather early break. This allows also to look at any addenda or corrections that have been filed and which are not known to the Chamber yet. So, therefore, if the parties would ensure, together with the legal officer, that the Chamber has received everything the parties wanted to submit, we'll look at it at the break. And then after the break, Mr. Margetts, you'll have the opportunity to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One thing, Your Honour. With respect to the Appeals Chamber decision, I would just encourage the Court, if it has the time to look at paragraphs 19 through -- basically through 21 again. Specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's always under my -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically related to the argument that the Prosecution had no obligation to notify of this -- the additional further clarification. And that's dealt with in the Appeals Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's the core of the decision. Mr. Kehoe, anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just on that score, I believe that approximately 30 of the 53 autopsies that counsel is attempting to put in, I do believe are -- bear on the appellant decision and the obligation of the Prosecution to notify the Defence as soon as possible which is something they have yet to do. So it is virtually -- well in excess of half of them are going to come into play specifically on paragraph 20 of the appellant decision says, The obligation resting upon the Prosecution to name the alleged victims to the extent possible, logically implies that it should do so as soon as practical after obtaining the information in order to facilitate the preparation of an effective Defence. That simply is response to the comments made by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic has already invited us to read 19 to 21. And 20, as far as I'm aware of, is just in the middle of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, in terms of the pleading of the Defence, I just looked at paragraph M and the final sentence that you referred to me to regarding 65 ter 6050, the cause of death is also unknown. I, in fact, differ with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will check that. And you will understand that if we get some 30 -- late at night if I open my mailbox at home and read this, I have not the entire underlying documents available. But you draw our attention to the fact that in M you consider that the report on the cause of death is inaccurate. Mr. Kehoe, there I would like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If can I refer my learned friend. As I understand it, 65 ter 6050, P1689 refers to autopsy report G04, 30B, which is referred to in Dr. Baccard's report at page 75 and the autopsy report of 2nd November, 2002, of Davor Strinovic concludes that the cause of death was blunt force head trauma or explosive head injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is interesting because the charging document that you have included where it sets forth the cause of death in virtually all of them, expect those were unknown that the Prosecution left blank. So when it is unknown, they leave it blank but -- and they have done so with regard to this instance, so I take it from the Prosecution's position that they have no idea why this person died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the way in which the Prosecution presents the results is guiding you, rather than the original material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, both. I will tell you, the original material, because I'm not sure what other material they have. And I'll give a case in point: They have charged in this document, in their -- in their schedule that an individual was killed in Donji Lapac on the 5th, for instance. Now if you look through the documents of the autopsies, it doesn't say anything about the 5th. But I assume that the Prosecution has done additional investigation to come to the conclusion that this person was killed on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the example, I'm not dealing with other matters that we have looked at already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that does go directly to the issue of notice. Because if on the schedule, these things are all left blank, and then in the autopsy report, it says unknown, I mean that -- and the schedule which we received in July and the autopsy reports which we did not receive, I believe, until October, I'm not sure exactly when we got the reports, but when we got Dr. Baccard's original exhibit list and with all the reports, I think that came some time in October, I mean, that goes directly to the issue of notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, all of this material was available to the Defence from April 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That is absolutely not the case. All of this material was not available to the Defence since April of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the situation is we've looked at the disclosure, a CD that was intended to include all of the material and did include 90 percent or more of the material was provided in April 2007. Now, the second issue is that then on -- in e-court the material was uploaded, and the references to that material was made very clear, and all the Defence had to do was to call us to supplement that disclosure. It was, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you've got to be kidding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you say that all -- that means 90 percent was available and all would have been available if the Defence would have called you to make it available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a puzzle which I think for to us consider during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in our submission, it was effective disclosure, and it was understood by us from disclosure records we had that all of the material was provided to the Defence. It has been in their possession for over a year, all of it, and we say, effectively disclosed to them for almost two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you say to the extent it was to be found somewhere that this is not effective disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my daughter would call that an egg-hunt, to try to decipher what the Prosecution was trying to present. We will go through chapter and detail concerning the disclosures on these autopsies and their deficiencies coming from the Office of the Prosecutor. I will present those to them. It -- it is simply not accurate what was just been said to this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The difference of view is clear, and it's now also clear why Mr. Kuzmanovic would like to spend the Easter weekend at home. We will have a break, and we will resume in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday two motions were filed. One was motion to exclude the evidence of Dr. Eric Baccard. That motion is denied, reasons to follow. Although not exactly the same matter, different, perhaps not totally unrelated, motion to reconsider filed yesterday, to reconsider the 25th of November decision. That motion will be decided in due course. The Chamber is working hard on decisions that will have to be taken as a result of the decision of the Appeals Chamber. The Chamber was pleased to hear that it was not expected that we do that in a hurry, and it might even be necessary to come back to the parties for some factual details before we finally decide on that matter, but we're working hard on it, but we have not yet finished. As far as the exhibits are concerned in relation to the next witness to be called, it has been emphasised, it has been stressed that there is a relation between these exhibits and the decision still to be taken as a result of the Appeals Chamber decision. Final decision on admissions will not be taken. Exhibits will be marked for identification, apart, of course, for any exhibit that is already in evidence. There, perhaps we would have to reconsider; we'll deal with that. The Chamber expects and the Chamber intends to finally decide on admission more or less simultaneously with the other decisions still to be taken, and the parties should not expect that we give any final decisions on admission prior to these other decisions. Whether we make it deciding the matter simultaneously is still to be seen. But that is at least what we're trying to do. Mr. Margetts, if you let me finish first, and then if there's any -- any questions, we'll hear from you. Finally, the parties are invited to deal with any exhibits on the basis of a proper understanding of what an expert can tell us and what he can't tell us. We do not expect whatever is there on paper that an expert, who, at a certain moment in time, is involved in exhumations or post-mortems, that he would know any specifics about circumstances under which the person died, which are not a result of his expertise in looking at the bodily remains. So whether someone died at 3.00 or 4.00, apart from where perhaps a watch has been shot at the same time, and then still it's to be seen this is more forensic expertise than the expertise of this witness. But there's no need it ask the expert, Is it true that you have no knowledge of this? Is it true that you have knowledge of that? And, Mr. Margetts, you're invited to positively establish what the expert can't tell us, and that should not take too much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you earlier were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I note that in respect of the reconsideration of the decision, you suggested that you may or may not invite submissions from the parties. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Invite submissions from the parties on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Further factual bases that may be relevant to the further consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In so far as a decision is rendered in regard to the clarification, we may -- on the basis of that decision, we should have put further submissions in relation to the relevance of the documentation. And so at this stage, I just indicate it may be preferable from the Prosecution's point of view if the issue of the further clarification and the issue of the admission of the documentation were not decisions that were rendered simultaneously, but if the further clarification decision could be rendered and possibly an opportunity for the parties to then put further submissions as to relevance of the material, having had the opportunity to consider the further clarification decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're inviting to us to kind of a second round on the relevance after we would have decided the clarification issue and reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm just minded to the fact that the clarification, the relevance of the clarification is clear. If the clarification is in any way changed, we may wish to put additional submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just as an officer of the Court, the submission that we made, I recognise that the motion has been denied, and I'm not re-arguing that; however, we went back through, and I noticed a couple of errors in the submission that we made. I know it has been denied, but in the spirit of accuracy, I'll just file a corrigendum -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that would assist us, especially later when we have to decide on admission, then, of course, it is welcomed if you -- if you would bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Margetts, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we're ready to call our next, Dr. Eric Baccard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I was informed that Mr. Baccard would not be available to continue next week but only the week after that. Well, that being the situation, of course, the parties are even more -- but I take it that we'll not finish with the witness today. That's at least my expectation. But there is no possibility then to hear his evidence early next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We made the inquiry also with the witness, and he indicated that he wouldn't be available to continue the testimony on Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Baccard, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, whole truth, and nothing butt truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Baccard, you will first be examined by Mr. Margetts. Mr. Margetts is counsel for the Prosecution, as you most likely aware of already. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Baccard. Dr. Baccard, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Eric Baccard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could bring up 65 ter 6032 onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, if you could look at the screen on the left there, can you confirm that that is your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Could you scroll it down and move it to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, one small question for Dr. Baccard. [Interpretation] Mr. Baccard, you're being shown a text in English. Can you tell us that you have a sufficient master of the English language in order to be in a position to answer questions on -- regarding an English document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. In the course of the years, I have learned some English, and I have a good knowledge of English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you don't have any problems with English text, and if you do, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could move to the third page of the curriculum vitae, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Baccard, having reviewed the three pages, are you able to confirm that that is your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, if we could please have an exhibit number and Dr. Baccard's CV could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, I confirm on the basis of your CV that you're a forensic pathologist of 27 years standing and that you're currently engaged by the Office of the Prosecutor at the International Criminal Court in the position of forensic coordinator for the Office of the Prosecutor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. I work as a coordinator of the forensic and criminalistic activities at the ICC, not the ICTY. So it the ICC, International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please go to the second page of Dr. Baccard's curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Baccard, I'd like to refer you to the middle of the page. And there's a reference there in the middle or just below the middle that refers to -- to the fact that you were president of the French Wound Ballistic Society until 1999. And then under that there are details in relation to various positions that you were engaged in acting for and on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. And I'd first like to refer to the reference to your activities in 1999. Would you be able to explain to the Court the role that you played as a forensic pathologist for the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in 1999.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in the autopsies carried out in Bosnia in Visoko in July 1999 as a forensic pathologist and then in Croatia, at the mortuary of Zagreb of the Salata hospital in November and October 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baccard. And if we could go down a little bit further, there's a reference to your engagement as the chief pathologist of the Office of the Prosecutor between March 2000 to November 2000. Are you able to explain to the Trial Chamber the tasks that you undertook in that position and the various remains and the location that those remains were exhumed from that you studied in that position.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The activity that I carried out in 2000 as chief forensic pathologist of the Office of the Prosecutor for the ICTY was in the first place to set up a morgue with two post-Mortem rooms and seven autopsy tables and then was charged to supervise the operation of this morgue where you had multi-cultural, multi-disciplinary teams with anthropologists, forensic pathologists, dentists, radiologists, and we had to work on the corpses that were exhumed in various sites in Kosovo in the course of the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate to the Trial Chamber, if you remember, approximately grave sites in Kosovo the remains that you examined were exhumed from and approximately how many victims you and your team examined?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I can't really come up with very precise figures. But it's over 225 autopsies that were carried out in this mortuary in Orahavac in the south of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1500. Correction of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I also worked with the mortuary which was in the British sector in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baccard. And then further down from the we have a reference your engagement as a forensic consultant from February 2001 to October 2002, again for the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. And can you confirm that one of the assignments that you undertook in this capacity was leading an ICTY, Office of the Prosecutor, ICTY monitoring team of autopsies that were conducted by Croatian pathologists in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct. The monitoring team including myself, of course, but there was also an investigator and a photographer, an officer who was also a scene of crime officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the autopsies that you monitored in this role where -- of remains that had been exhumed from three sites; Korenica, Rizvanusa, and Gracac. And the autopsies were conducted between May and June 2002, and then, later, during September and October of 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now subsequently to the monitoring mission, you were asked by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY to prepare an expert report, and you prepared an expert report in relation to the -- your monitoring of the autopsies and reviewing the autopsy reports that were produced by the Croatian team in June 2003. And that report related to the Korenica and Gracac sites. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Baccard, on Monday of this week, you met with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and you were shown a copy of that report from June 2003 that had been redacted by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. And you were given the opportunity to compare that report, where parts have been redacted or taken out of it, with your original report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could please have 65 ter 7038 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Baccard, this is a lengthy document of some 137 pages. So I'll just show you the first page. And can you see there, is that the page that you signed on Monday?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, again, Dr. Baccard, is that your signature and the date reflecting Monday's date that appears on this, which is the final page of that redacted report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could please have an exhibit number. This could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, marked for identification as Exhibit P2314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, that report that I have just shown you, can you confirm that that report that you saw, the redacted report that you saw and signed on Monday, accurately reflects the findings that you came to, having monitored the autopsies and having reviewed autopsy reports, in relation to the various victims that are referenced in that report for the Gracac exhumations?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of the cases that were redacted, yes, this is indeed the very same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question in this request, Mr. Margetts. You introduced in your question the word "victim." Findings on bodily remains may sometimes or perhaps often not give a possibility to identify whether they were victims. They were persons who had died. When we're talking about "victims," can I take it, Dr. Baccard, that we're talking about the bodily remains of the persons who were the subject of the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, if we could please have 65 ter 7048 presented on the screen. Mr. President, it appears that we have a technical difficulty in locating 65 ter 7048 in e-court. If I could just a moment while my assistant attempts to remedy that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. It still hasn't been uploaded in e-court. I think we can do it via Sanction; it might be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it is not uploaded. I do have a hard copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel, I have it on Sanction. I can put it on Sanction right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

And that's just for the benefit of the parties and the Trial Chamber. When you're examining the remains and seeking to ascertain cause of death, can you explain to the Trial Chamber precisely what the -- the range of findings you can make are. In other words, are there any limits, in terms of the extent to which you can describe circumstances or cause of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It's a very wide question, and I may give you a long answer. As you know, when one carries out an autopsy, it is to determine the cause and the circumstances of death. The cause of death can only be confirmed after a whole series of examinations, and this is various procedures which will look at the state of conservation of the body, and this may create a limit to the autopsy. Then we have to see which identification elements can be drawn up, whether -- to see whether it was a male or female, if there any other characteristics such as scars, tattoos, or other. And afterwards, there is an inventory that's made of various injuries. And among those various injuries, we can find injuries that are benign, and other injuries are more serious. And can you also find injuries that can be considered as being potentially deadly. And after establishing this inventory of wounds, one can come to a conclusion as to the cause of death. One can, for instance, have a victim or a person that's deceased who received -- who is injured at the hand, for instance, and there's a another person -- or if the same person received also a bullet at the heart, of course, the cause of death is not the bullet found in the hand of the person but the bullet found in the heart because there is a cardiac arrest. And so the determination, the cause of death, is only concluded at the end of the autopsy. And then of course one has to determine the circumstances of death. And the circumstances of death can be only -- the conclusion can be only made after examining various elements, whether it -- there's a whole slough of elements that one can find, whether it is an entry wound behind the head, or if you could see that a person was shot at point blank, whether there is an multiple lesions or dramatic lesions. All this can eventually help us conclude why the person died. So, of course, you're asking me whether there are limits to this exam. Obviously, if the body is deteriorated -- the more the body is deteriorated, the more the conservation of the body is bad, and the forensic pathologists will not have sufficient elements to come to these conclusions. Of course, it is it much easier to find the cause of death, but the circumstances of death are much more complicated. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I please ask you to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I was saying the conclusions that one can draw as to the circumstances of death are usually made after a more refined analysis, and it is based on various indicia. It is much more difficult to find out the circumstances of death than the cause of death. As to the other limits, there are other limits, and they are linked to the fact that a corpse may be whole or not. We can sometimes only find body parts and that, of course, if -- if 80 percent of the body is missing, the forensic pathologist will have a lot of trouble to determine the cause of death, unless if, for instance, he has a skull in his hands, and there was a projectile injury at the skull. So to have the entire body is an important element. The conservation of the body is also an important element, and this is why we are very often called to use various sources of information, whether it is photographs taken at the inhumation. But it is also the X-rays, the X-ray photographs are very important. And this can show us small elements that cannot be seen during the autopsy because of small fragments that can be found there, and that are all inside the putrefied parts. And so the radiography, the X-ray is very important because we can see the small elements. Also the examination of clothing is very important, and obviously one can make a difference or one can come to a conclusion whether a person was injured by a projectile or because of an explosive. If you have a burst of small shrapnels, and you can see that at a leg, and you have only one only entry point in a pair of trousers, this will help to us understand, of course, aside from the small shrapnel fragments, but this will be able to show us that there was one projectile that entered and then fragmented, for instance. So all these elements are taken into account when the forensic pathologist is analysing the causes of death and the circumstances of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baccard. In terms of the time of death and when the person died, what observations can a forensic pathologist make that would assist them in ascertaining time of death, if they are in fact able to ascertain time of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: We are able to evaluate, of course, always approximately the time of death when we intervene very rapidly after the death of the person. But as time goes by it is more difficult to put a date to a death of a person with certainty and this is, of course, linked to the non-specific character of putrefaction, and also other factors that can influence putrefaction. For instance, how big the body is, whether the body was dressed or not, the nature of the earth where the body is inhumated, whether there is water that is around that area where the person is found, whether there was plastic bag around the body, whether there was a coffin, so all this influences the putrefaction factor. So during the examination we were not able to also carry out entomological examinations such as the presence of various insects and larvae on the body. If this examination was not carried out, it would not -- it's -- it's completely incorrect to try to put a date as to the death of bodies that were exhumed many years later.
