utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Baccard, we will have a break. After the break, we'll further discuss your availability, because we might not finish today and, unfortunately, this Chamber is not sitting tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, and we were informed that you are not available next week. So we'll discuss that after the break. But we'll first now have a break until 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Baccard, it's Mr. Kuzmanovic who will begin the cross-examination. He's the Defence counsel of Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. I'd just like to take you back to the end of your testimony in your direct examination, where you were discussing putting a date of death on the bodies that you were involved in reviewing. And you said on page 55, line 14 and 15: "It's completely incorrect to try to put a date as to the death of bodies that were exhumed many years later." My questions to you in this portion of my cross-examination relate to that statement. Is it fair to say, based on your testimony, that in this particular case to conclude a time of death or a date of death would be speculative?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: There is an translation error. I indicated the term illusory that has been translated by incorrect. What I, in fact, meant to say was that over and above a certain lapse of time, it is not scientific possibly to establish with certainty a date of death, and it is even truer for the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Doctor, that in this particular instance, meaning in the review of the exhumations and the -- in your expertise as a forensic pathologist, it would be speculative to conclude a date of death for any of the autopsies that were performed in this case?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Firstly, the expertise I performed no expertise or examination I performed. I acted only as an autopsy performer. If by performing an exhumation, what does not allow us, if we do not perform examinations in terms of the presence of insects, that does not allow us to determine the date of death. If the body has remained at all times in the same environment before being buried, we can have a better estimate. But the fact that of burying the body and then exhumating the body does not allow to determine the date of death with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, in this case, it's fair to state, had nothing to do with where -- in what part of Croatia these bodies were found. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't understand the question translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, have you done no investigation, and you were not asked in any form to provide information about the location of where these bodies were found prior to their burial. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No. I just know -- I just knew the name of the site where they were exhumated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I ask that, Doctor, is there have been representations made in this case with respect to specifically the bodies that are referred to in these autopsy reports of generally a place where the body was found and a date given as to approximately when the death occurred. And I'm asking you, as a forensic pathologist, and I think you have confirmed that you cannot tell us or you were not asked to tell us about where the body was found, and you could not as a forensic pathologist determine the date of death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us when the last time you, yourself, performed an autopsy?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Last Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's something that you do on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: This is that I did on a regular basis, up until my arrival at the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the autopsy -- you don't have to get into any details obviously. Was that performed in your role as a -- at the ICC?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before your work at the ICC and the autopsy that you performed there, when was the last time you had performed an autopsy as a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The year 2007?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you -- in your report which is P2314.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if I could have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 4. And there was some discussion about this. Actually, Judge Orie asked you a question about this and that I wanted to follow up on. Section 3, background of the report. The first sentence in that paragraph says: "The monitoring mission of the autopsies of the victims exhumed ..." And my question to you is, was it your presumption when performing these -- this review -- and for purposes I'll say what you did was a review, rather than you, yourself, did not commit -- conduct autopsies. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was only there to observe the autopsies that were performed by the Croatian pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So when I'm referring to your work, Doctor, I'll just refer to it as your review, just so we're clear. During your review, Doctor, you had presumed that all the persons that were exhumed from these particular sites were victims of some kind of a crime?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question mark, that happens now and then in cross-examination. Something is put to you, and then in the translation the question mark more or less disappears, but that's how --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kuzmanovic spoke this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, did you presume when you conducted your review that the people that -- upon whom the review were conducted were all victims of a crime?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I observed autopsies conducted on exhumed bodies in sites for which I was given the name, but like all experts, I have no a priori as regards the particular situation of the body that i have before me. It is only after the expert examination that the circumstances of death appear or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you list the members of the Croatian forensic team on page 4 of your report. Can you tell us -- were you at all critical of any of their work in this process, other than what you've written in your reports, in terms of disagreeing with certain analyses?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It's certain that I would perhaps not have conducted the autopsies overall in the way in which they were conducted. Notably I would not have fractionated the various times of the examination. I would have no doubt have assembled on a single day the radiographic examination, the forensic exam, the anthropological exam, the examination of the clothing so as to be able to have at the same time all the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did not reflect upon the seriousness with which they took their work. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't understand -- what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You were critical of certain methodologies, but that did thank did not reflect upon them in terms of the seriousness with which they undertook their work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of your report, Doctor, at the top, you do state under methodology that the methodology adopted by the Croatian forensic team was generally -- the word says "conform;" but I would think it would be in conformance with the international scientific standards. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be possible to display page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. You'll see at the very top under 4.1, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In answer to your question, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 6 of the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You -- in the first full paragraph that starts: "The main problem." You discuss that there was a -- there were possible gaps in the chain of custody, and you had explained that briefly in the answer to a previous question. Would you agree with me, Doctor, that the possible gaps in the chain of custody did not affect the report -- reports written, autopsy reports written, and your analysis of those reports?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I believe, that is, that we asked the Croatian pathologists to secure the rooms where the autopsies were being conducted, to secure the rooms where the bodies were stored, and the room where the clothing was washed and dried. And, therefore, I believe that, given the fact that Professor Strinovic and myself each had a set of keys, that we could consider that the place was secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the problem that you address on page 6 about possible gaps in the chain of custody, as far as you're concerned, did not affect the overall result here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7, Doctor. As it's coming up on the screen, you describe the composition of -- and you term them victims groups. And you note civilian or military status in that particular section. "The status was affirmed only when several typical pieces of uniform were present." Now, can you -- can you expand on that and discuss that and give us an indication of what -- what you felt was necessary to determine whether someone was civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Indeed, this is what is described in my observation report. The items of uniform were generally the upper part and the lower part. The forensic experts didn't just base themselves, for example, on the presence of boots or rangers' boots but required a complete uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could pull up P1692, please. And while that's coming up, Doctor, would remnants of ammunition be considered evidence of someone holding military status?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the second page of this document, under section E, there is an radiologist finding: "In the projection of the head, we can see a head with three entire bullets as well as the metal bullet frame." And if we go further into the document. Unfortunately, mine are page numbers, so you will have to bear with me for a moment. If you go to page 8 which is the artefact listing, the first artefact listed is a bullet in the thorax, and the second artefact listed is three live rounds in the skull area. And if we go to the next page, which are the smaller radiographs, we have what looks like a clip of three bullets. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That is indeed what we see on the X-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if those bullets were fired from a weapon, they would not look like that in the skull of a -- someone who was exhumed from a grave, would they not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No. I believe here there's a confusion. These rounds are not in the skull but are a projection in the area that was X-rayed at the same time as the skull. That is why the presence of rounds or a clip -- live rounds does not constitute as such an indication of belonging to a civilian or military group. The identifying garment must belong quote/unquote "to the body." During an exhumation the earth around the body may contain just any object, and it's not because the persons who performed the exhumation at the same time put items that are close to the body that said items necessarily belong to the body. There is a distinction to be made, and I repeat, that the criteria that were used by Croatian experts to decide on belonging to the civilian or military group were only based on the fact that said persons were clothed in uniforms. In other words, these uniforms were around the bodies. They hadn't put them on. Same as for the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, in essence, Doctor, you discounted the fact that there was a live clip of ammunition near this person as bearing any factor on whether or not there person was civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Indeed, that did not come in as part of the criteria that were used by the Croatian experts, and quite rightly, because we don't know whether this clip was in the same position in the burial site or whether it was picked up from underneath, or what its origin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, back to your report, page 7. Just as a general question, Doctor, concerning the issue of bullet entry wounds and bullet exit wounds. Nowhere in any of the reports is it shown whether bullet entry wounds were caused by a short-barrel weapon or a long-barrel weapon. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You understand, do you not, that the same calibre bullet could be fired from a short-barrelled weapon as could be from a long-barrelled weapon? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It depends on the projectiles, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There are several places in various analyses of reports that you have done that have concluded or hypothesised that there was a bullet entry wound or a bullet wound that was a cause of death, but nothing more specific than that. Correct? Meaning about the type of weapon or the type of calibre bullet or something like that, unless an artefact was found.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It's also possible in lesional ballistics, wound ballistics to have indications that are derived from the appearance of lesions caused by high-speed bullets, different from those from medium- or low-speed projectiles. We can distinguish between wounds caused by AK-47 rounds and a 9 millimetre round. It is quite possible, and we have to look at the wound profile, what we call the wound profile, the way in which the projectile will interact with the tissue when we're fortunate in still having soft tissue, or, if not, the way in which the projectile will perforate the bounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to state that the kind of analysis that you just described wasn't possible because of the state of the remains, correct, generally?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Except when we obtained characteristic impact on -- bone surface. But generally speaking, it was difficult to specify the wound profile given the state of tissue degradation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could please go back to page 7 of your report, which is P2314. You state, Doctor, on page 7 under the forensic criteria conservations status, the last sentence that that section: "This criterion was important to know in order to determine the degree of liability of the autopsy's findings." What I'd like to ask you is, what do you mean by the degree of liability? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That is depending on the state of preservation of the body, we will have more or less information available to us, in order to determine the nature of the wound suffered. Here we have a body that is reduced to skeleton state. Everything that is surrounding the -- for the missing soft parts we will have to limit our examination to only one of the constituents of the body. When we have greater tissue thickness, there we have far more information stemming from the ballistics examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess for my own benefit, when you say "degree of liability," would you mean degree of accuracy? Or am I wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's the degree of completeness of the findings that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now later on in this page, there's a discussion regarding point of entry, and at the bottom of the page, there's a discussion about the characteristics of the projectile have been noted when it was possible. And then it goes on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which I would ask the registrar to move to, please, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "This information being generally absent on the reports of the Croatian experts." And then you have the schematic of the body at various positions. My question to you is: Who was the person or persons who determined the path and trajectory, if it was not done by the Croatian experts?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The path or trajectories that are in my report of autopsy attendance are trajectories that I determined based on my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the angles and the entries and the exits were all determined from your notes that you did yourself?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As regards the angles, yes. As regards the point of entry and point of exit, this information which can be found in the Croatian forensic's experts, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us earlier that your notes that you had regarding this particular analysis or investigation, you don't have or can't find anymore. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 25 to 30 percent of your questions are either seeking, That's what you wrote, is that what you wrote? Or trying to get the same answer two or three times, apparently because you consider them important. Could you please try to be as focussed as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the next section you discuss cause of death. And it might seem trivial, but you use the term "the cause of death was established," and it seems to me that there were potentially several causes of death that were considered in many of these reports. What was it that led to you conclude about "the" cause of death as opposed to "a" cause of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In actual fact, if you read the very last paragraph, I say that the cause of death was established taking into account the potentially lethal wounds. And in some cases, several possible cause of death were identified, and putrefaction did make it possible to determine which was the particular wound that led to the lethal fate of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's true that there is no specific cause of death listed as homicide in any of the reports. Correct? Or circumstance of death, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this is a question to be addressed on a case-by-case basis, based on the various autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And doing as such on a case-by-case basis, at least you have not come to any determination that any of these reports concluded that that was a result -- the death was the result of a homicide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, homicide, is that a legal term, or is it anything else? Isn't homicide killing with intent another person or not with intent, depending on what kind of homicide we're talking about? Of course, if you want to ask this expert whether he came to any conclusions in terms of intent or whether someone killed by a bullet; it was an accident, that one of his children fired a weapon by mistake or -- is that the area? Because homicide is typically a legal term, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't-- I didn't use it, Your Honour. It's in his report. He is the one who put it in his report, and he is the one who used it in his report, so that's why I'm asking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you did not come to any determination that any of these reports concluded that death was as a result of a homicide. Yes. You couldn't, isn't it? But it's just our understanding of what the expertise of this witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think that it's any -- it's a useful line of questioning, then -- just -- I just want to draw your attention to the fact that whoever uses whatever terminology that it seems to be very much legal expressions, opposed to anything I consider this witness could tell us about, not knowing anything about the circumstances, as he said before. The only thing he knew is the site where the -- the name of the site where the bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess my question related to his comment that the manner or circumstances of death was noted when this determination was possible. And one of the manners or circumstances he listed was homicide. And my question to him was, were any of these reports listing homicide as a manner or circumstance of death? And his answer was that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he never concluded that, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 33 of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we close some microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the top of page 33 of your report, Doctor, you disagreed with a conclusion of a specific report, and you state in the second sentence: "Indeed several arguments are supporting the hypothesis of gunshots." Now two questions I have regarding this sentence. The first is the subject of arguments. Do you mean facts, or are you being an advocate here on the issue of disagreeing with Mr. Strinovic's report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I certainly do not claim to be an advocate of any sort. I base myself on forensic and medical -- or facts in order to do exactly what I was called upon to do, which was to monitor what the Croatian forensic experts were doing and to give my opinion in this respect, and my findings are based on what I monitor. In this particular case, I was in disagreement with Professor Strinovic. At the time of the autopsy, we discussed it together. And at the later stages of the forensic examinations, i.e., the examination of pieces of clothing and the analysis of X-rays, all of this support my opinion. I believe that this was not explosive injury but an injury caused by the fragmentation of a projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, isn't it -- it's true, is it not, that based on your disagreement with Professor Strinovic, that his view was also a reasonable one as much as yours was based on the arguments that he made? Two reasonable people can disagree. Correct.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I believe that my colleague, Professor Strinovic, is a perfectly reasonable person and is somebody who is respectable, somebody who has very good forensic education. However, in this particular case, we were in disagreement. I argued in favour of my findings. I presented four forensic arguments, and I continued to believe that my assumption is scientifically valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just as his is; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, in my report, I said that his assumption was not scientifically valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The use of the word "hypothesis," and it's used in several places in your report, Doctor. A hypothesis implies that there is insufficient evidence to provide more than one tentative explanation. And it seems to me that in many instances, especially in incidents where you hypothesised there were execution killings, that there is insufficient evidence to confirm there were or there were not those types of killings. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: So what is your question exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is when you use the word hypothesis, that is not something that can you conclude to a reasonable degree of certainty. That's speculative. You are speculating that there was an execution-style killing based on the evidence that you have before you. Not that in fact occurred?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I never spoke -- I didn't speak of execution. The point of disagreement with Professor Strinovic regarded the causes of death. He said that a death was due to explosive injury, and I said it was due to gun-shot projectiles. This has nothing to do with the circumstances of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 54, Doctor, of your report. If you look at the second paragraph of this part of your report, you state with respect to this particular case: "The gun-shot was directed from back to front, slightly downward. It was consistent with the hypothesis of an 'execution-style' shot." Now before I had asked you about the use of the word hypothesis. And would you agree with me that a hypothesis is generally an assumption or a concession made of an argument?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that on the issue of your use of the term hypothesis of an execution-style shot would be speculative?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It's one hypothesis. The autopsy is a piece of the puzzle that the magistrate has at his or her disposal and that has to be assessed with the other elements of the expertise. But we have to present all the various assumptions or hypotheses that can be arrived at after our examination of the corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But a hypothesis is not a conclusion of the manner of death; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I said, I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 97 of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the lower part of the document, where you discuss some disagreement with Professor Strinovic's report. You describe a -- this particular fracture as "consistent with a blunt-force trauma possibly caused by a weapon's butt." Now, the sole basis for you to make that conclusion was because there was a ping-pong fracture?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The point of disagreement only concerned the precise location of the trauma of the fracture. Professor Strinovic was mentioning the temporal area which is much lower and on the side of the skull, while the impact, as you can see on the picture, was located in the left parietal bone. So the point of disagreement with Professor Strinovic was only concerned with the location. Now we're dealing here with a typical fracture of a trauma caused by a blunt force. As to the semi-circular shape and the dimension as well as the characteristics are compatible with the hypothesis of a fracture caused by a weapon butt. I -- several times in Kosovo as well, I was able to observe this type of trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at any time, Doctor, when you were involved in reviewing those autopsies -- I'll strike that question. This kind of injury that you just described and that we just referred to could also have been caused by someone falling from a significant height. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The location of this fracture, which is located on the upper and lateral part of the skull, and also due to the shape of the depression, this is not really compatible with this hypothesis. Now, if there is a priority to be given to the various options, I wouldn't give the fall of a person as being the top priority that would come to mind, in view of this particular fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page 99, please. If we go to the bottom of page 99, 5.2.119.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a discussion here about an injury which you disagreed with initially, and you described that "the injury was with pellets likely fired by a shotgun." Now, were you aware at any point in time that any military personnel in Croatia used shotguns?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't get this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you concluded that the injury was not related to a hand-grenade but something fired by -- pellets fired by a shotgun. Can you explain for me how you came to that conclusion, that it was pellets from a shotgun?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. In this particular case, this is not a hypothesis, but it is an absolute certainty. And if I could have the photographs and the X-rays, I could demonstrate to the Court on what basis I came to this finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exhibit number handy, but I will take your word for it, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you may, if I may, sorry. This was absolutely characteristic. You can see the pellets that are in -- into the surface of the bone, so obviously we're not dealing with fragments coming from a hand-grenade. We're dealing with spherical pellets, lead pellets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I would say that it was compatible with lead. There was a greyish trace when you touched it. But, of course, there was no analysis carried out, or if such analysis were made, they were not brought -- they were not brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... possibility that it might have been gravel or some kind of pellets from rocks? You know where the territory of these -- of this area of operation that occurred is very rocky and very -- has a lot of areas where gravel are contained in the roadways. Did you exclude that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. This possibility can be excluded definitely. The diagnosis of such lead pellets fired by gun-shot are confirmed by the X-rays. Everything that is made of metal is shown in a very dark colour on X-rays. The colour contrast is very clear. Nothing to do with the colour of gravel, for instance, and the shape of these pellets was regular, spherical, all of the same dimension. And I'm sorry we can't be shown the pictures taken in the course of the autopsies or the X-rays, where I wouldn't need to make it any further comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 136, please. Okay. Sorry, that's been redacted. If we could go to 137, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: During the course of your direct examination, you had -- in an answer to a question, you had mentioned the term "scene of crimes officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually we don't need this page anymore, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me what you meant by that? That's how it was interpreted anyway?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, in actual fact, these scene of crime officers were part of our team, and they were there as forensic photographers. They were also acting as an officer protecting evidence, recording evidence, describing evidence. They were also describing the pieces of clothing. So this officer had a dual role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Was this a Croatian person? Or was this an ICTY person? Who was this scene of crimes officer?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In our team we included a scene of crime officer, but essentially we had two persons. I think that in the Croatian team, if my memory serves me well, because I can't really remember precisely, but I think they also had a police officer, but I can't be absolutely certain of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, how many of these -- did you personally see all of the autopsies that were performed, observe them?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At least all those that are listed in my monitoring report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then what did you do after the autopsies were completed? Did you then go back and write your own report? Did you wait for somebody else to write a report? Can describe for me what you did.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I was then writing my notes. I was comparing my point of view with that of my Croatian colleagues, and then I was checking with our photographer or scene of crime officer that the appropriate photographs had been taken, and we would make an appointment with the autopsy -- the Croatian autopsy assistants, in order to examine the pieces of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We had already discussed to some extent the fact this is an lot of room for interpretation in these reports and that there's also a lot of room for the reports not being definitive one way or the other on the issue of cause of death. For the most part, you agreed with the findings of the autopsy reports of the Croatian pathologists. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With the few exceptions that I have already mentioned in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then when you list a cause of death as unknown or, for example, the Croatian pathologist lists a cause of death as unknown, at least at that point in time, you had not -- or no one had sought any additional information to try and fill in that gap to change it from unknown to some gun-shot, or grenade, or anything like that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, that's more or less true. The Croatian pathologists based themselves on the autopsy findings, and I also took into consideration the examination of the photographs and the pieces of clothing, realizing the limitations of hypothesis one can draw from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will look over my notes. I'm just about done. There's a question I have, but it would be directed to Attorney Margetts, so it really is -- I would want to ask him before i ask the witness. It has to do with the redactions, Your Honour. The reason I say this is we got the redacted report relatively recently. And I, of course, had marked up the non-redacted report, and some questions I had were involving areas where there were redactions. So I would like to ask him about that before I conclude my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the questions you want to put if the witness would hear them and would hear the answers, would that in any way prejudicial to -- possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think would be better if the witness removed his headphones, and I just went to chat with Mr. Margetts, just for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because if you stay at a distance, he would understand everything, yes. So perhaps he could better keep his earphones on, which is even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you were -- could consult with Mr. Margetts more closely, then you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had enough questions to take me through the rest of the day based on the redactions, which are now redacted, so I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. It also gives me an opportunity to express that, in all fairness, I had overlooked the use of the word "homicide," although it nowhere materialised any further on. And that what I put as a question to you and perhaps with a -- in a tone which might not have been the appropriate one, that perhaps it should have been addressed to someone who used that word in this context where it's unclear whether it could mean anything more than a legal concept. I just want to put this on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No offence taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who is next in line for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, mine is next. I do believe, in fairness to the witness, I mean, taking him back and forth without some continuity, and that it's going to be difficult, and I don't think I am going to finish in this period of time. I think it would be quicker if I went from start to scratch as opposed to going through it and having some five, six, seven days down the line just rehashing what we did before, just to bring it back into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I feel obliged to observe that Dr. Baccard is someone whose time, particularly at this moment in this month is at an absolutely premium, and we have had some problems with scheduling his evidence, and we obviously don't want any time that he is attending these premises to be wasted, and so we would say given that consideration, it would be far better from our point of view if this time was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I inquire with the Cermak Defence team whether they have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber is not fully convinced yet that it would save time so invites to you start your cross-examination. [Interpretation] Mr. Baccard, the next counsel who will cross-examine you is Mr. Kehoe, and he defends Mr. Gotovina. Cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor, it's a pleasure to meet you. Doctor, I would like to ask you some general questions, and I think that you can probably move through some of this quickly. And I think you did touch upon it in response to some questions by Mr. Kuzmanovic. But I think you would agree, Doctor, that the fact that these bodies were in the ground for several years, that they were in an advanced state of decomposition and many had skeletal remains, obviously made your analysis and the analysis by the Croatian pathologists very difficult. You would agree with that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I do believe, I think you've touched on this just a bit with Mr. Kuzmanovic when you were answering some questions generally about being a forensic pathologist with the experience level that you have, that generally when you're doing a forensic examination and coming to a conclusion in an autopsy, you have tissue and organs, and based on an analysis of damage to tissues and organs, you can make a more thorough conclusion as to the cause of death. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. But the forensic pathologist has to often give conclusions on bodies which are quite decomposed, yes. We -- we are used to working with bodies that are often very much damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But it makes your ability to render accurate conclusions concerning the cause of death, for instance, more difficult when you're faced with merely skeletonized remains or maybe skeletonized remains with minor degrees of saponified flesh. It makes it more difficult to make that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And just to wrap this up, that is also because you have skeletonized remains, you can look at things such as bruising and wounds in the flesh to make determinations concerning, say, bullet-holes or maybe a knife wound or something of that nature. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct. When we examine remains that are skeletonized, we can only see what is present at the bone level. Everything -- if everything else has disappeared, we cannot conclude anything as to the disappeared flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, if you just have skeletonized remains, you can't make a determination whether or not an individual died from natural causes, such as disease, heart attack, something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct. Unless the illness touches the skeleton itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Let me -- I'd like to ask you a couple of questions based --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that page 80, line 16, that there's -- that you intended to say, You can't look at things as, because the witness confirmed that it was correct, but in view of the question, I think it needed some clarification, like in your next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Could we turn to P1251, which is the report of Dr. Clark. And if I could turn to page 4 of this document, which is 235. Three pages up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph in deciding -- this is Dr. Clark's report, and he is deciding -- breaking it into various areas, and the paragraph is dealing with decided whether a particular finding was genuine or not, and he writes: "With discoloured and broken down tissues assessments such as things as bruising, wounds, or bullet-holes in the skin was extremely difficult, and in many cases impossible, as the changes seen could have been part of the normal post-mortem process." You agree with that, do you not, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And staying with that concept of post-mortem and pre-mortem processes, oftentimes it is very difficult to make a decision when you are looking at skeletonized remains whether that particular injury that you may see to a skeletal structure took place antemortem or post-mortem. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It is it more difficult, but it is not impossible, especially if you are dealing with bleeding, which can happen at the level of the factors, for instance, or the defect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's stay with that just a little bit. If we're talking about hemorrhaging or some type of bruising, you wouldn't be able to examine those types of things in skeletonized remains, you would have to have some type of flesh to see that type of wound, would you not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It is it not quite true because if you are talking about hemorrhage or the ecchymosis, it leaves the traces on the -- on the skin, on the flesh, and then you can see that there was a blood collection at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Doctor, that is assuming you have skin. And most of the bodies that you looked at didn't have skin, right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No. But I'm talking about the colouration of the surface of the bone. Let's talk about the skull. You can have a collection of blood that can disappear after putrefaction, but you can have a colouration on the bone which shows that previously there was a blood collection that is it now gone because of the putrefaction. It is it all a matter of case-by-case analysis. It is very difficult to draw conclusions or rules when we talk about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A translation issue. I was listening to the French. Could I invite to you look at your screen where the text appears, and look at page 82, lines 7, 8, and 9. Could it be that you said something different in French as to where the traces were to be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said is that in some cases we can still see on the bone surface the print of a hemorrhage that took place when the wound touched the bone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, let's just take this post-mortem and pre-mortem analysis yet further. You were doing these exhumations in 2007 with bodies that had been in the ground since approximately mid-1995, or the latter part of 1995. And when you were examining these bodies with the Croatian forensic pathologists, did you notice various damage, items of damage to the skeletonized remains that you concluded were post-mortem type of damage?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In many cases, the lesions were attributed to a post-mortem traumatism whether it's during the exhumation, maybe a shovel hit or something like. And also there are certainly also traces of various scavengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the scavengers. I didn't see that in your report. I mean, what kind of traces of scavengers did you see?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I was not referring to that type -- to this in my examination. When you have post-mortem traumatisms, you can also -- you have to take into account also scavenging, but I do not address those issues in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that, generally speaking, you have to take into account scavengers when you're looking at post-mortgage damage, you didn't necessarily conclude that there was scavengers in this particular situation; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. It was a general answer regarding possible origins of various post-mortem lesions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that. If we can go back to this report by Dr. Clark on number 2, he is dealing with post-mortem damage. And he notes in his examination, and this is a different scenario. This is a different cemetery. He notes that dealing with the latter, post-mortgage was certainly a consideration and something that could have occurred in a number of ways. In the process of handling the bodies and putting them into graves in the first place from the pressure of compacted soil or other bodies over the years or from the final process in exhuming them. I know that that's somewhat of a limited list. Would you agree that those are all possibilities, that post-mortem damage could occur to a corpse and/or to skeletonized remains?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Taking this from Dr. Clark's experience and bringing it to yours, I'm interested in the amount of post-mortem damage that you observed going through these autopsies, because I read how that your report, and I didn't see any indications of post-mortem damage. Do you recall during your report -- maybe I missed it. And pardon me if I did, Doctor, with all due respect, I may have missed it. But do you recall listing when you were going through here what you considered to be post-mortem damage when you're assessing the injuries either to the skeleton or to a corpse?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I believe that I must remind you that my report is a monitoring report. It's a report of a monitor. I was present there in order to give my opinion on the quality of work undertaken by my Croat colleagues, and this is not an expertise report. This is a report drafted by an expert on an expertise that I did not carry out myself. And to answer to your question as to post-mortem or antemortem lesions, this is in the report of the Croat forensic experts, some squares are checked, post-mortem damage or antemortem damage is checked. So these are elements taken into account, but I, myself, did not have to make any this particular observation as to this. My report was rather an internal report. It was made for the OTP, and I never thought, or I did not think that it would be produced subsequently to the Chamber. And this is not an expertise, a report, I draft expert reports that are completely different. This is a technical report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware that we have to deal with some scheduling issues as well. So I wonder whether this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first part of the scheduling issues, I would like to deal with in the presence of the witness. Dr. Baccard, I was informed that you are not available, that you have a lot of work to do next week. Mr. Kehoe, could you tell us how much -- how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, a few hours. I think a little bit more than a session. Session an a little bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours. Now, I appreciate, and I fully respect if you have no two hours available next week, Dr. Baccard. If, however that would be different, if you say, Well, I'm not available for a whole day or for two days, that is fully understood. Your unavailability would also be firm if we are talking about half a morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a matter still to be -- still to be considered then. If you would say, Certainly not on this day, but I might find could or three hours on another day, then we might try to find -- because we have -- we are not fully booked with witnesses next week to say the at least and, of course, if we try to lose as little time as possible. I would like to hear from you whether three hours would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is going to be very difficult. Because I have to answer an order by the ICC, and they are ordering me to compile three expert reports by next Friday. And last week, there was this mission to Africa, and I do not think that I will be able to free myself for half a day next week. However, I'm entirely at your disposal next week at any date, for any date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from exploring the possibility, but your answer is you couldn't find close to half a day next week. I'm -- I hardly dare to ask, but you say have you to deliver those reports on Friday? Is that Friday close of business? Because ... would there be any time remaining on Friday? [Microphone not activated] [Previous translation continues] ... and, if not, of course, we're ... May I take your silence as an expression of being perhaps a bit unpleasantly surprised by this question? Is that a proper understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I understand very well. However, I cannot tell you right now, knowing all the work that's awaiting, that's ahead. But maybe next week at the beginning of the week, I would be able to give you some answer depending on how much I'm advanced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... whether you would have possibly another job to do next week as well. So we leave that for the time being. Mr. Margetts, was I correctly informed if you would like to ask the witness to come back on the 16th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be, I have to look at my court schedule in the morning hours or... perhaps Mr. Registrar could help us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be available on the 16th of February, in the morning, that is, 9.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for being available on that date. You're invited to then join us in the same courtroom on Monday, the 16th of February, and from what I hear, it will not taking more than half a day. I would further like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, either the testimony you have given already today or still to be given on the 16th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Usher to escort Dr. Baccard out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I do understand that, due to health issues, that you have not -- not your health, that no witnesses are available until Thursday. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Unfortunately so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is very unfortunate. Because we are not being able to use five days in court, which is -- which is to be deplored. If there is no other procedural issue in relation to scheduling at this moment, we adjourn, and we'll resume on Thursday, the 12th of February, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of February, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 25
